title: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
summary: Make an RNN's hidden state a small model trained by gradient steps as it reads. Derive the delta rule as one step, parallelize with mini-batches, then add Titans' surprise, momentum and forgetting.
outcomes: Explain how a TTT layer turns the update rule into one gradient step on a self-supervised key-value loss
Derive the delta rule and linear attention as online versus batch gradient descent on the same loss
Compute memory writes, retrieval errors and the effect of mini-batch size on a small example
Explain Titans' surprise, momentum and forget gate, and how MAC, MAG and MAL combine memory with attention
Weigh the costs of learned memory: wall-clock, stability, chunk size and when to keep attention

lessons.title: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading

blocks.md: From the prerequisite course you know two ways to carry context. Softmax attention keeps every key and value (the KV cache), so recall is exact but each new token costs time proportional to the context length. Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet compress the past into a fixed matrix state, so each token costs the same, but the state can only hold so much.

The TTT paper (Sun et al., 2024) shows what that limit looks like. On long Books documents, a Transformer's average perplexity at token position $t$ keeps falling all the way to 32k tokens, because later tokens condition on more context. Mamba's curve flattens after about 16k: past that point the extra context stops helping. The authors' diagnosis is that the update rule is a poor *compression heuristic* for thousands of tokens.

Their key observation: we already know an excellent compression heuristic. Training a model with self-supervised learning squeezes a huge dataset into its weights while keeping the structure that matters, which is exactly what pretraining does to an LLM. So treat the context as a small unlabeled dataset, make the hidden state the **weights** $W$ of a small model $f$, and make the update rule **one step of gradient descent** on a self-supervised loss.

blocks.title: Three layers, one template: state, update rule, output rule

scenes.caption: Every sequence layer fits one template: a hidden state, an update rule that writes the new token into it, and an output rule that reads it to produce z_t.
Naive RNN: the state is a fixed-size vector and the update squashes old state plus new input. Cost per token is constant, but everything must fit in one small vector.
Self-attention: the state is the KV cache, a list that grows by one entry per token. Nothing is compressed, so recall is exact, but each output scans the whole list.
TTT layer: the state is the weights W of a small model f. The update is one gradient step on a self-supervised loss; the output runs f on the token. Fixed size, but a learner instead of a buffer.

labels.upd: W = W - eta x grad loss

blocks.tex: W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta \, \nabla \ell(W_{t-1}; x_t), \qquad z_t = f(x_t; W_t)
blocks.caption: Update rule (one gradient step with inner learning rate eta) and output rule (run the freshly updated model on the token).

blocks.md: Because this training keeps happening on every test sequence at inference, the layers are called **Test-Time Training (TTT) layers**. Two instantiations appear in the paper: **TTT-Linear**, where $f(x) = Wx$, and **TTT-MLP**, where $f$ is a two-layer MLP with hidden size 4 times the input and a GELU. In both, $f$ is wrapped as $x + \mathrm{LN}(f_{\text{res}}(x))$ (a LayerNorm and a residual connection) for stability.

Which loss? The naive choice is denoising: reconstruct $x_t$ from a corrupted copy. The paper instead *learns* the task. Three learned projections give a **training view** $\theta_K x_t$, a **label view** $\theta_V x_t$ and a **test view** $\theta_Q x_t$. The inner model learns to map the training view to the label view, and the output reads the model at the test view. The subscripts are deliberate: these play the roles of key, value and query.

blocks.tex: \ell(W; x_t) = \big\| f(\theta_K x_t; W) - \theta_V x_t \big\|^2, \qquad z_t = f(\theta_Q x_t; W_t)
blocks.caption: The multi-view reconstruction loss of TTT. In the inner loop only W is optimized; the thetas are fixed hyperparameters of the loss.

blocks.md: There are now two nested learning problems. The **inner loop** trains $W$ on the current sequence. The **outer loop** is ordinary language-model training: it learns $\theta_K, \theta_V, \theta_Q$, the initial weights $W_0$ and the rest of the network with next-token loss, backpropagating through the inner gradient steps. This is learning to learn (meta-learning), which is where the paper's title comes from.

blocks.title: Inner loop trains W; outer loop trains everything else

scenes.caption: A new sequence arrives. Every TTT layer resets its state to W_0, which is shared across sequences and learned during training.
Inner loop: token by token, W takes a gradient step on the self-supervised loss. Only W changes here, and it is thrown away when the sequence ends.
Each W_t makes the layer's output z_t. Later layers turn these into next-token predictions.

Outer loop (training only): backprop through the inner gradient steps, which means gradients of gradients, to update the projections, W_0 and the rest of the network. At inference the outer params are frozen but the inner loop still runs.

blocks.md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

TTT here does not mean fine-tuning the LLM on your prompt. The network's ordinary parameters stay frozen at inference. Only the small per-layer weights $W$ change, they start from $W_0$ for every sequence, and they are discarded afterwards, just like an RNN's hidden state.

One more consequence of the gradient view, quoted from the paper: $W$ remembers inputs that produce large gradients, intuitively the inputs that make $W$ learn a lot. Keep that in mind; Titans turns it into an explicit design principle called surprise.

blocks.question: During inference with a TTT model, what changes as the model reads a long prompt?
options: Nothing; all weights are frozen at inference
Only the inner weights W inside each TTT layer, which act as a per-sequence hidden state
All model parameters, via backpropagation of next-token loss on the prompt
The projections theta_K, theta_V and theta_Q, which adapt to the prompt
blocks.explain: The inner loop runs at inference, so each layer's W takes gradient steps on its self-supervised loss. The outer parameters (projections, W_0, the rest of the network) are learned in training and frozen. No next-token loss is backpropagated at inference.

blocks.question: Why does a TTT layer have constant cost per token while softmax attention does not?
options: Its weights W have a fixed size no matter how many tokens were absorbed, while attention's KV list grows by one entry per token and must be scanned
TTT skips tokens with small gradients, so it processes fewer tokens
TTT uses a sliding window over the last 16 tokens
Attention recomputes the whole prefix from scratch for each new token
blocks.explain: The cost of an update or read depends on the state size. W stays the same shape forever, so each step costs the same; attention's state is the KV cache, which grows linearly, so reading it costs O(t). Attention does not recompute the prefix (the cache prevents that).

lessons.title: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule

blocks.md: Make everything as small as possible. Let the inner model be linear, $f(k) = Wk$, and ask it to map keys to values with half the squared error. (The TTT paper writes the loss without the one half; that only rescales the learning rate.) Here $k_t = \theta_K x_t$ and $v_t = \theta_V x_t$ are the training and label views from the last lesson.

blocks.tex: \ell(W) = \tfrac{1}{2}\| W k_t - v_t \|^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \nabla_W \ell = (W k_t - v_t)\, k_t^\top
blocks.caption: The gradient is an outer product: prediction error times key.

blocks.tex: W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta\,(W_{t-1}k_t - v_t)\,k_t^\top = W_{t-1}\big(I - \eta\, k_t k_t^\top\big) + \eta\, v_t k_t^\top
blocks.caption: Expanding the gradient step gives the delta rule: erase what W currently stores along k_t, then write v_t along k_t.

blocks.md: One step of online gradient descent on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

A worked example in 2 dimensions with $W_0 = 0$ and $\eta = 1$ (the paper's *base* inner learning rate for TTT-Linear; in practice it is scaled down by a learned sigmoid gate, and the official code also divides it by the head dimension). Three writes arrive: key $(1, 0)$ with value $(2, 1)$; key $(0.6, 0.8)$ with value $(-1, 1)$; then key $(1, 0)$ again with a *new* value $(0, 2)$, as if a fact in the document was updated. Both keys have length 1.

blocks.prompt: After the third write, what will W return for key (1, 0)? And will key (0.6, 0.8) still return its value (-1, 1)?
blocks.reveal: Key $(1, 0)$ returns exactly $(0, 2)$: with a unit key and $\eta = 1$, the factor $(I - k k^\top)$ wipes the old association along that key before writing the new one. Key 2 does **not** survive intact: it now reads $(-1.408, 1.456)$. The keys overlap (dot product 0.6), so correcting key 1 also moved key 2. A $d \times d$ linear memory can only store about $d$ independent associations cleanly.

blocks.title: The memory W after each write (eta = 1, unit keys)

scenes.caption: Start: W_0 = 0, so every key reads back (0, 0).
Write 1, key (1, 0) to value (2, 1). Prediction (0, 0), error (-2, -1), loss 2.5. The step adds (2, 1) along key dim 1; reading key 1 now gives (2, 1) and the loss drops to 0.

Write 2, key (0.6, 0.8) to value (-1, 1). W currently predicts (1.2, 0.6), error (2.2, -0.4), loss 2.5. The step subtracts the error along this key, so both columns change. Key 2 now reads exactly (-1, 1).

Write 3 overwrites key (1, 0) with new value (0, 2). W predicts (0.68, 1.24), error (0.68, -0.76), loss 0.52. Only column 1 changes because the key points along dim 1. Key 1 reads (0, 2): the old fact is replaced, not blended.

blocks.title: TTT-Linear inner loop on the three writes
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
W = np.zeros((2, 2))         # hidden state = weights of f
eta = 1.0
pairs = [((1, 0), (2, 1)),
         ((0.6, 0.8), (-1, 1)),
         ((1, 0), (0, 2))]
for k, v in pairs:
    k, v = np.array(k), np.array(v)
    err = W @ k - v           # prediction error
    W = W - eta * np.outer(err, k)   # one gradient step
    print(W @ k)              # read the key back

scenes.caption: The state starts as a zero matrix. In a real TTT layer it starts at the learned W_0.
Write 1: the error is prediction minus target. The gradient of half the squared error with respect to W is the outer product of error and key.
Write 2 with an overlapping key. The step corrects the prediction along k = (0.6, 0.8), touching both columns.
Write 3 reuses key 1 with a new value. The update erases the old association along that key and writes the new one.

blocks.title: Inner loss before and after each gradient step

scenes.caption: eta = 1 with unit-length keys: each step removes the whole error along the key, so the loss after every write is exactly 0 (an exact overwrite).
eta = 0.5: each step halves the error, so the loss falls to a quarter (2.5 to 0.625, 1.525 to 0.381, 0.967 to 0.242). The learning rate is how hard the memory writes.

blocks.md: Now compare plain linear attention, which updates $W \mathrel{+}= v_t k_t^\top$ and never subtracts. The TTT paper's Theorem 1 shows this is also a TTT layer: a linear model trained with **batch** gradient descent, every gradient taken at $W_0 = 0$ (with their unhalved loss, $\eta = 1/2$). Each token's gradient is then just $-v_t k_t^\top$, so the state is the running sum.

blocks.title: Reading keys back after all three writes

scenes.caption: Cells 1 and 2 read key 1 = (1, 0); cells 3 and 4 read key 2 = (0.6, 0.8). Key 1's correct value is the latest one, (0, 2).
One-step-at-a-time gradient descent (the delta rule) reads key 1 exactly. Key 2 drifted to (-1.408, 1.456) because the keys overlap (dot product 0.6): fixing key 1 nudged key 2.
Linear attention just adds v k-transpose each time and never subtracts the old value. Key 1 reads (1.4, 3.6), a blend of all three values. This is the memory overflow that the delta rule fixes.

blocks.md: So the difference between linear attention and the delta rule is the optimizer, not the architecture. With **online** gradient descent, $W_t$ is $t$ steps away from $W_0$ and each step sees what is already stored. With **batch** gradient descent, $W_t$ is effectively one step from $W_0$, so it cannot notice that a key already holds a value.

blocks.question: A TTT-Linear layer uses keys with squared length 4 (not normalized) and inner learning rate 0.6. The same key-value pair is written five times. What happens to the error along that key?
options: It shrinks to zero after the first write, like with unit keys
It shrinks by a factor of 0.6 each write
It flips sign and grows by 1.4 times each write, so the memory diverges
It is unchanged, because repeated writes of the same pair cancel
blocks.explain: Each step multiplies the error along k by (1 - eta x |k|^2) = 1 - 0.6 x 4 = -1.4. Starting from an error of -1, the five writes leave 1.4, -1.96, 2.744, -3.842, 5.378. Stability needs eta x |k|^2 below 2, which is why practical layers normalize keys (Titans L2-normalizes queries and keys) and learn or gate eta.

blocks.question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
blocks.explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention.

lessons.title: Making TTT fast: mini-batch gradient descent and the dual form

blocks.md: The update $W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta \nabla \ell(W_{t-1}; x_t)$ cannot be parallelized over tokens: $W_t$ depends on $W_{t-1}$ both before the minus sign and inside the gradient. Training on 2048-token sequences would mean 2048 dependent steps per layer, each a tiny matrix-vector product that leaves a GPU idle.

The TTT paper's fix uses an idea from ordinary training: **mini-batch gradient descent**. Split the sequence into blocks of $b$ tokens. Every gradient in a block is taken at the weights from the end of the previous block, so the $b$ gradients are independent and run in parallel. The weights inside the block are then a cumulative sum of those gradients.

blocks.tex: G_t = \nabla \ell(W_{t'}; x_t),\quad t' = t - (t \bmod b), \qquad W_t = W_{t'} - \eta \sum_{s=t'+1}^{t} G_s
blocks.caption: b = 1 is online GD (the delta rule); b = T is batch GD (linear attention when f is linear and W_0 = 0). The paper uses b = 16 everywhere.

scenes.caption: Online GD (b = 1): each gradient needs the W produced by the previous one, so 8 tokens take 8 dependent steps. Simplified model: one wave of parallel gradients costs one time unit.
Mini-batch GD with b = 4: the 4 gradients in a block are all taken at the W from the end of the previous block, so they run in parallel. 2 dependent waves instead of 8.
Batch GD (b = T): one wave, maximally parallel, but every gradient is taken at W_0. That is linear attention, which we saw cannot overwrite.

blocks.md: Run the three writes from the last lesson with different block sizes to see what is lost. With $b = 2$, writes 1 and 2 share a block (both gradients at $W_0$) and write 3 starts a new block, so it sees the accumulated state.

blocks.title: Same three writes, different mini-batch sizes: retrieval loss

scenes.caption: Key 1 (correct value (0, 2)). With b = 1 or b = 2, write 3 is computed from a W that already stores key 1, so it overwrites cleanly: loss 0. With b = 3 every gradient uses W_0 and key 1 reads (1.4, 3.6): loss 2.26.
Key 2 (correct value (-1, 1)): loss 0.187 for b = 1, 0.418 for b = 2, 2.34 for b = 3. Bigger blocks mean fewer real steps and worse memory.
Total loss over both keys: 0.187, 0.418, 4.6. Smaller b buys quality with sequential work; larger b buys parallelism with quality.

blocks.md: The paper measured the same tradeoff at scale: smaller $b$ gives lower perplexity because the inner loop takes more real gradient steps, while larger $b$ allows more parallelism until the hardware saturates. Its ablation table shows how much the optimizer choice matters relative to everything else.

blocks.title: From linear attention to TTT-Linear (125M, perplexity)

scenes.caption: Table 1 of the TTT paper: start from linear attention at 15.91 perplexity and add one component per row. Lower is better.

The biggest single gain (-1.70) is switching from batch GD over all 2048 tokens to mini-batch TTT with b = 16. The second (-1.22) is LayerNorm plus residual inside f. Learnable W_0 slightly hurts (+0.04) but the authors needed it for stable training.

blocks.md: Mini-batching is necessary but not sufficient. Each $G_t = 2(W_0 x_t - x_t)x_t^\top$ (identity projections, the paper's unhalved loss) is a $d \times d$ outer product: $b$ separate outer products are not one matmul, and materializing $b$ matrices of size $d \times d$ costs memory traffic. The **dual form** computes the block's end weights and all its outputs without ever forming the individual $G_t$ or $W_t$.

blocks.tex: W_b = W_0 - 2\eta\,(W_0X - X)X^\top, \qquad Z = W_0X - 2\eta\,(W_0X - X)\,\mathrm{mask}(X^\top X)
blocks.caption: X stacks the block's b tokens as columns. mask keeps entries with s at most t (an upper-triangular mask with zeros, like a causal attention mask but zeroing instead of using minus infinity).

blocks.md: Cost per block: $O(b d^2)$ for $W_b$ plus $O(b^2 d)$ for the outputs, slightly more than the primal form's $O(b d^2)$, but all matmuls. With $d$ in the hundreds and $b = 16$ the extra term is small, and the authors report training more than 5 times faster than the primal form in JAX. Training and prefill use the dual form; decoding, which is sequential anyway, uses the primal form. A quick numerical check on a random 4-token block with $d = 4$: primal and dual agree to within $4.4 \times 10^{-16}$, pure floating-point rounding.

If the dual form looks familiar, it should: the masked $X^\top X$ term is the same structure as chunkwise linear attention, with a within-chunk causal mask plus a carried state. TTT generalizes it to any differentiable inner model (the appendix derives the MLP case).

Later work argued the other way. *Test-Time Training Done Right* (LaCT, 2025) notes that TTT layers with $b$ of 16 to 64 often use below 5% of a GPU's peak FLOPs. For a fast-weight matmul of an $h \times h$ weight with a $b \times h$ chunk in BF16, the best possible compute-to-memory ratio is $r = \frac{hb}{h + 2b}$, which never exceeds $\min(h/2, b)$.

blocks.title: Arithmetic intensity of one fast-weight matmul

scenes.caption: Small fast weights (h = 64) with small chunks (b = 16) do about 10.7 FLOPs per byte moved, far below the roughly 290 an H100 needs to be compute-bound. The GPU waits on memory.
The ratio can never exceed h/2 or b, so growing b alone saturates at 32 for h = 64. Small states are memory-bound no matter how you batch.
LaCT's recipe: wide fast weights and huge chunks. With h = 1024 and b = 2048 the ratio is 409.6, past the balance point, so the matmul is compute-bound.

blocks.question: You raise the TTT mini-batch size from 16 to 2048 in a TTT-Linear language model and change nothing else. What do you expect?
options: Lower perplexity, because larger batches give less noisy gradients
No change in quality; b is purely a speed knob because the dual form is exact
Faster training per step but worse perplexity, since the inner loop now takes far fewer real steps (b = T is batch GD, close to linear attention)
Slower training and better perplexity
blocks.explain: The dual form is exact for a given b, but b itself changes the algorithm. The TTT paper's ablation shows smaller b improves perplexity because W takes more gradient steps; b = T collapses to batch GD. LaCT gets away with huge chunks only by adding window attention, wider nonlinear fast weights and a different update rule.

blocks.question: What does the dual form change about a TTT layer?
options: Its outputs: it is an approximation that trades accuracy for speed
Only how the same outputs are computed: matmuls replace per-token outer products, and the intermediate G_t and W_t are never stored
The loss: it switches from reconstruction to a dot-product loss
The order of updates: it processes tokens right to left
blocks.explain: The paper stresses that primal and dual forms are equivalent in output. The dual form spends a bit more theoretical compute (an extra O(b^2 d) term) to get matmul-friendly operations and avoid materializing b matrices of size d x d.

lessons.title: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory

blocks.md: *Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time* (Behrouz, Zhong and Mirrokni, Google Research, December 2024) keeps the TTT recipe and asks what a good long-term memory needs. Its memory $\mathcal{M}$ is an MLP with $L_\mathcal{M} \ge 1$ layers. Keys and values come from linear projections of the token, and the inner loss is the same associative-memory regression as before.

blocks.tex: k_t = x_t W_K,\quad v_t = x_t W_V, \qquad \ell(\mathcal{M}_{t-1}; x_t) = \big\| \mathcal{M}_{t-1}(k_t) - v_t \big\|_2^2
blocks.caption: Reading is a forward pass without any weight update: y_t = M*(q_t), with q_t = x_t W_Q.

blocks.md: Titans names the gradient **surprise**: a large gradient means the token is far from what the memory predicts, so it should be stored strongly. Plain TTT already does this. The paper's worry is what happens after a big surprise: the gradient can quickly become small, and the tokens right after an important event get written weakly even though they belong with it.

The fix splits surprise into a **momentary** part (this token's gradient) and a **past** part (a decaying running sum), which is gradient descent with momentum. A forget gate then shrinks the memory before each write, which is weight decay on $\mathcal{M}$.

blocks.caption: eta_t: how much past surprise carries over. theta_t: how much of this token's surprise to use. alpha_t in [0, 1]: how much memory to forget. All three are computed from the token.

blocks.md: Each gate has an interpretable extreme. $\eta_t \to 0$ ignores the previous surprise (useful at a change of context); $\eta_t \to 1$ keeps it fully. $\alpha_t \to 0$ leaves old memory intact; $\alpha_t \to 1$ wipes it. The paper also shows the parallel training trick from the last lesson extends to this rule: chunked gradients at the block start, decay factors folded into matmuls, and the momentum recurrence computed with a parallel associative scan.

A toy run makes the dynamics concrete. The memory is a single number $M$, every key is 1, the loss is $\frac{1}{2}(M - v_t)^2$ so the surprise is $M - v_t$, and $\theta = 0.4$. The values are 2 for three tokens, then the context switches and they become $-2$ for five tokens.

blocks.prompt: At token 5, right after the switch, will the momentum version write a larger or smaller update than plain gradient descent?
blocks.reveal: Larger: $|S_5| = 1.841$ with momentum versus $0.856$ without. Momentum keeps pushing in the direction of the token 4 surprise, so the memory adapts to the new context faster. The cost is overshoot: memory reaches $-2.854$ at token 7 against a target of $-2$. Adding the forget gate ($\alpha = 0.1$) reduces the overshoot to $-2.493$.

blocks.title: Scalar memory reading a context switch at token 4

scenes.caption: Plain gradient descent (no momentum, no forgetting), theta = 0.4. Values are 2 for three tokens, then the context switches to -2. The surprise spikes to 3.568 at token 4.
Plain GD: after the spike, the surprise shrinks each token (2.141, 1.284, ...), so writes shrink too. By token 8 memory is only at -1.723 of the new target -2.
Momentum eta = 0.5: the update S_t carries past surprise forward. At token 5 the write is -1.841 instead of -0.856. Memory reaches -2.325 by token 6, overshooting the target.

Momentum plus forgetting alpha = 0.1: each step first shrinks M by 10%. The overshoot drops from -2.854 to -2.493, and the stale value 2 fades faster. In Titans all three gates are computed from the token, not fixed.

blocks.title: How long a write and a surprise survive

scenes.caption: With alpha = 0.1 a stored association keeps 0.9 of its weight after 1 token, 0.349 after 10 and almost nothing after 100, if nothing rewrites it. Momentum 0.5 forgets surprise within a few tokens.
alpha = 0.01 keeps 0.904 after 10 tokens and 0.366 after 100: long retention. Titans makes alpha depend on the token, so it can hold steady within a topic and dump memory at a boundary.
alpha = 0.5 halves memory every token: effectively a very short window. alpha near 1 would clear it entirely.

blocks.md: Why an MLP instead of a matrix? A matrix memory $W$ trained on $\|W k - v\|^2$ is online linear regression, so it assumes the past is linearly related to its keys. The authors argue deeper memories store more: in their experiments raising depth from 1 to 4 lowered perplexity at every sequence length, while training throughput fell roughly linearly with depth. Depth is a quality versus speed knob.

blocks.title: Titans ablation: removing one piece at a time (perplexity)

scenes.caption: Table 5 of the Titans paper, neural memory alone (LMM). Lower is better. The full module scores 27.01.
The largest losses come from removing weight decay (29.04, the forget gate) and momentum (28.98). Swapping the deep MLP memory for a linear one costs 1.48 perplexity.

blocks.md: Strip Titans down to a linear memory with no momentum and the update becomes $W_t = (1-\alpha_t)W_{t-1} - \theta_t (W_{t-1}k_t - v_t)k_t^\top$: a delta rule with a forget gate. That is the same family as Gated DeltaNet from the prerequisite course, and the paper presents its decay as a generalization of the forget gates in Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet. Titans' additions are the deep memory and the momentum.

Surprise is not a separate score or probability the model predicts. It is the inner-loss gradient itself, the same quantity a TTT step already uses. Likewise $\eta_t$ here is momentum *inside the memory's inner loop*; it has nothing to do with the outer optimizer (AdamW) that trains the network.

Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

blocks.question: In the Titans update, the model sets alpha_t close to 1 at some token. What does that do?
options: Writes this token's value with maximum strength
Clears almost all of the memory before adding the current update
Freezes the memory so this token is ignored
Carries all of the previous surprise into this step
blocks.explain: alpha_t multiplies the old memory by (1 - alpha_t). Near 1 that wipes the memory, which is useful at a hard context boundary. Write strength is theta_t; carrying past surprise is eta_t.

blocks.question: Which change would you expect to hurt the Titans neural memory most, according to the paper's ablation?
options: Removing the persistent memory tokens
Removing the 1D convolutions after the projections
Removing weight decay (the forget mechanism)
Replacing SiLU with GELU in the projections
blocks.explain: Table 5: without weight decay perplexity rises from 27.01 to 29.04, the largest drop, with momentum next (28.98). Persistent memory matters least (27.63). The activation swap was not tested, so the paper gives no evidence for it.

lessons.title: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs

blocks.md: A neural memory alone is a full sequence layer, but Titans argues for pairing it with attention. Attention is precise but limited to its window, so it acts as **short-term memory**. The neural memory keeps learning from everything it has seen, so it acts as **long-term memory**. A third piece, **persistent memory**, is a set of $N_p$ learned tokens prepended to the input: they hold knowledge about the task, do not depend on the input, and do not change at test time.

blocks.title: Three ways Titans wires memory and attention together

nodes.label:
Neural memory M
(learns at test time)

scenes.caption: The pieces: attention as precise short-term memory, the neural memory as long-term memory, and persistent memory, a few learned data-independent tokens that hold task knowledge and stay fixed at test time.

Memory as Context (MAC): split the sequence into segments. Query the memory with the segment, prepend the retrieved h_t and the persistent tokens, run full attention inside the segment, then use its output to update the memory and gate the final output.
Memory as Gate (MAG): no segmenting. Sliding-window attention (with the persistent prefix) and the memory read the same input in parallel, and a nonlinear gate mixes their outputs.

Memory as Layer (MAL): the common hybrid stack. The memory layer processes the input (with persistent prefix) and sliding-window attention runs on its output. Simplest, but each layer limits the next.

blocks.md: In the paper's language-modeling runs (340M to 760M parameters, 15B or 30B tokens of FineWeb-Edu) all three Titans hybrids beat the authors' Transformer++ and recurrent baselines. At 760M, WikiText perplexity was 25.21 for Transformer++, 21.18 for Gated DeltaNet, 20.04 for the memory alone, 19.93 for MAC, 18.61 for MAG and 19.07 for MAL. MAC did best on long-dependency tasks. These are one group's runs at small scale; treat them as evidence for the mechanism, not a ranking.

blocks.title: Single needle in a haystack (S-NIAH-W, accuracy %)

scenes.caption: 2K tokens. Numbers are from the Titans paper's Table 2 (RULER benchmark, the paper's own small models). Already a spread: TTT 78.8, Mamba2 42.2, DeltaNet 46.2, Titans LMM 90.4, MAC 98.2.
4K tokens: TTT falls to 28.0, Mamba2 to 4.2, DeltaNet to 20.0. Titans LMM holds 89.4, MAC 98.2.
8K tokens: TTT 4.4, Mamba2 0.0, DeltaNet 1.6, Titans LMM 85.8, MAC 95.6.
16K tokens: the three baselines are at 0.0; Titans LMM 80.6, MAC 95.2. The authors credit forgetting and momentum versus TTT, and deep memory plus the ability to remove memories versus Mamba2.

blocks.md: The same paper reports Titans scaling past a 2M-token context window with higher needle-in-haystack accuracy than baselines. The paper's efficiency section is candid about cost: the memory module trained slightly slower than Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet, which have highly optimized kernels, while MAL was the fastest Titans variant because most of its work is FlashAttention.

**Large chunks instead of small ones.** *Test-Time Training Done Right* (LaCT, Zhang et al., 2025) attacks the hardware problem from lesson 3. It updates fast weights once per chunk of 2K to 1M tokens, uses window attention to model order inside each chunk, and spends the saved efficiency on a much bigger state: a SwiGLU MLP fast weight up to 40% of the model's parameters, versus 0.1% to 5% in earlier designs. It replaces weight decay with L2 normalization of the updated weights, can use the Muon optimizer for the inner update, and reports up to 70% GPU utilization on A100s in a few dozen lines of PyTorch.

LaCT's chunk order also changes what the memory can see. If a chunk applies the weights before updating on itself, a token's TTT output only reflects earlier chunks, never its chunk-mates. That shifted block-causal pattern avoids leaking future tokens in language modeling, and it is exactly why local attention is needed inside each chunk.

**Real uses beyond text.** LaCT adapted a 14-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer into an autoregressive generator for sequences up to 56K visual tokens, and ran novel view synthesis with more than a million tokens of context. *One-Minute Video Generation with Test-Time Training* (CVPR 2025) added TTT layers to a pre-trained 5B Transformer to generate one-minute cartoons from storyboards. In a human evaluation of 100 videos per method it led Mamba 2, Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window baselines by 34 Elo points.

**One map for all of these.** The Miras paper (*It's All Connected*, 2025) describes every model in this course with four choices:

1. **Memory architecture**: vector, matrix, or MLP.
2. **Attentional bias** (the inner objective): dot-product similarity for linear attention, L2 regression for DeltaNet, TTT and Titans.
3. **Retention gate** (forgetting): none for DeltaNet and TTT, an L2-style decay for Gated DeltaNet and Titans.
4. **Memory learning algorithm**: gradient descent, or gradient descent with momentum for Titans.

Common failure modes: (1) Wall-clock, not FLOPs, is the bottleneck. The TTT paper reports that TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, and Titans' throughput falls roughly linearly with memory depth. (2) Inner learning rates that are too large make the memory diverge (lesson 2). (3) Without forgetting, a fixed-size memory overflows on long inputs. (4) Most published comparisons use models under 1.5B parameters.

Learned memory turns the state of a recurrent layer into a model trained online. You choose its architecture, objective, forgetting and optimizer; you pay for expressiveness in wall-clock time, and you still pair it with attention for exact local recall.

blocks.question: You build a LaCT language model with 2048-token chunks and apply-then-update ordering, but you delete the window attention to save compute. What breaks?
options: Nothing; the fast weights still see every earlier token
Within a chunk, a token's TTT output only reflects earlier chunks, so tokens cannot use their nearby chunk-mates through the TTT layer
Future tokens leak into the past, so training loss looks too good
The model becomes quadratic in sequence length
blocks.explain: With apply-then-update, all queries in a chunk read the weights from the end of the previous chunk. That prevents leakage but means up to 2047 preceding tokens in the same chunk are invisible to the TTT layer. LaCT adds local window attention exactly to cover that within-chunk context.

blocks.question: In Titans (MAC) at test time, which part keeps changing its weights as the input streams in?
options: The persistent memory tokens
The attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V
All three, since Titans fine-tunes itself at test time
The neural long-term memory M
blocks.explain: The paper is explicit: persistent memory parameters stay fixed because they encode task knowledge, the attention weights are fixed in-context learners, and only the long-term memory keeps learning (memorizing) at test time.
